name: The Flynn Effect
statement: Measured IQ scores rose steadily across the twentieth century, about three points a decade.
meaning: Raw IQ test scores climbed substantially and steadily across successive birth cohorts through the twentieth century, on the order of three points per decade, adding up to roughly thirty points over a century. Because IQ is scored relative to a population — the average fixed at one hundred — the underlying gains only show up when old and new norms are compared, and tests must be periodically re-normed to keep pace.
mechanism: People did not become smarter in any everyday sense; average performance on the specific tasks IQ tests measure rose over time. Since the mean is pegged at one hundred for each standardisation sample, the raw-score gains become visible only when a test normed decades ago is given to people today, who then score well above the old average. The proposed causes — better schooling, greater test familiarity, improved nutrition, more cognitively demanding environments, reduced disease and lead exposure, smaller families — are many, and none is established as the cause.

examples.text: Gains are largest on culturally reduced, abstract-reasoning tests like Raven's matrices, where scores rose markedly over the decades — an uneven pattern that argues against a simple rise in general intelligence.
The Wechsler scales were restandardised in 1974, 1991, 2003, and 2014, each revision re-anchoring the average to one hundred for a contemporary sample, because scores kept drifting upward.

In several developed countries scores have stalled or declined since around the 1990s; a large Norwegian study found the rise peaked and then fell within families, pointing to environmental causes for both the gain and its reversal.

variants.name: The negative Flynn effect
variants.text: The documented slowdown or decline in average scores in several developed countries since roughly the 1990s, reversing the long twentieth-century rise.

variants.name: Fluid versus crystallized gains
variants.text: The uneven pattern in which gains are largest on fluid, abstract reasoning and smallest on crystallized knowledge like vocabulary — itself an argument against reading the effect as a simple rise in intelligence.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most important and puzzling findings in psychometrics, forcing the recognition that IQ scores are relative to their era and cannot be compared across decades without re-norming. It complicates claims about intelligence, heredity, and group differences, and its recent reversal in rich countries deepens the puzzle of what environmental forces drive it.

working.text: never compare IQ scores across eras without accounting for the drift, since old norms make modern test-takers look artificially high.
treat the gains as environmental and cohort-driven, but do not assert any single cause, since none is established.
read the rise as far too fast to be genetic, so it reflects changing environments, not changing genes.

limits: The score gains and the resulting need to re-norm are well documented, but the cause is unknown and debated — no proposed mechanism is established. The effect does not mean genes changed, since the gains are far too rapid for that, nor straightforwardly that each generation is smarter, given the uneven fluid-versus-crystallized pattern. And it has stalled or reversed in several developed countries since around the 1990s; a large Norwegian study found the decline appears within families, ruling out genetic selection or immigration and pointing to environmental drivers for both the rise and the fall. Most data come from developed nations, limiting generalisation.
misreadings: It does not show that people are becoming genetically smarter — the gains are too fast to be genetic and reflect changing environments. And it is not a permanent, universal climb: scores have plateaued or reversed in several rich countries in recent decades.
origin: Documented and popularised by James Flynn in the 1980s, and named 'the Flynn effect' by Herrnstein and Murray in The Bell Curve (1994); rising scores had been noted earlier by Runquist, Smith, and Tuddenham, and the reversal was analysed by Bratsberg and Rogeberg in 2018.
